To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the relative lake-level records of five late Holocene strand plains in Lake Michigan indicate that (1) the average time between ridge formation is 29 to 38 yr, (2) there is an approximately 30 yr lake-level fluctuation that is superimposed on the long-term loss of lake-level, and (3) the long-term lake-level trend has been a loss of lake-level of approximately 0.5 m over the past 5000 yr.
the relative lake-level record of the five strand plains shows a long-term loss and a 150 yr fluctuation in lake-level amplitude of ≈1 m.
strand plains in Lake Michigan contain a record of late Holocene lake level, and the record shows that lake levels fluctuate in response to a 30+ yr cycle and a 150+ yr cycle.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the timing of strand-plain development in Lake Michigan and the use of these data to reconstruct relative lake-level changes.
the timing of beach-ridging events in the Lake Michigan coastal plain and the use of beach ridges as a proxy for lake levels.
the development of strand plains and the recognition of lake-level changes in Lake Michigan.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Lake Michigan basin is currently losing water, but at an accelerating rate.
lake levels in the Lake Michigan system have been rising since the late Holocene and have been punctuated by short-term (30+ year) fluctuations.
the Lake Michigan basin has lost water since the mid-Holocene and has experienced lake-level variations on a 30 and 150 year cycle since 4700 yr BP.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
lake-level fluctuations in Lake Michigan are a combination of short-term (30–50 yr) fluctuations and longer-term (150 yr) variations superimposed on the long-term loss of lake water.
the Lake Michigan basin is responding to the long-term isostatic adjustment by a series of 150 yr lake-level fluctuations.
the lake level in Lake Michigan fluctuates by 0.5–1.5 m over a period of 30–150 yr, and the average rate of lake-level rise is 0.2 m/1000 yr.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the strand-plain record can provide a high-resolution, continuous lake-level curve for Lake Michigan.
the Lake Michigan basin is a sensitive recorder of lake-level change.
strand plains are sensitive to lake-level fluctuations and that the timing and magnitude of these lake-level fluctuations are consistent between sites in the basin.
